title: Coral Reefs Face Collapse in Next 50 Years, Say Experts
paragraphs: Almost all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face a very high risk of collapse within the next 50 years, according to a major new assessment.

The assessment was carried out by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and announced in October 2026 at a UN biodiversity conference in Albania. It is the first time that the IUCN's Red List, which is best known for measuring threats to species, has assessed coral reef ecosystems around the world. The assessment covered 127 tropical and subtropical regions and about 188,000 square kilometers of reefs.

The IUCN found that 96% of shallow-water reef systems are already critically endangered, its highest risk category, and could disappear by 2075. These include some of the world's most famous reefs, such as Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef and the reefs of the Red Sea.
A reef ecosystem collapses when the hard corals that form its foundation largely die and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. The reef can then no longer support its rich variety of life.

The IUCN described climate change as the single most consistent threat to coral reefs. Rising ocean temperatures and marine heat waves cause coral bleaching, which can kill corals. A survey a year earlier found that bleaching had affected 84% of the world's reefs. Pollution, overfishing and coastal development also damage reefs.
The 96% figure is based on future climate projections. If scientists considered only the past 50 years, 24% of reef ecosystems would be classed as critically endangered.
Coral reefs support about a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and provide food and tourism income.

However, experts say there is still hope. According to Mishal Gudka, the scientific lead of the assessment, the findings should be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair, because reefs have shown a remarkable ability to recover. Experts have called for major cuts in emissions, as well as stronger protection and restoration of reefs.
